Connivance means secretly allowing something wrong to happen by deliberately doing nothing about it.

The person who commits connivance is not the one doing the bad thing — they are the one who knows about it, could stop it or report it, but chooses to stay quiet and let it happen. They look the other way on purpose.

Think of it as silent permission for wrongdoing.

Three things must be true for connivance to exist:

  1. You know something wrong is happening. You are not ignorant. You are fully aware.
  2. You have the ability to stop it, report it, or speak up. You are not helpless.
  3. You deliberately choose to do nothing. This is the heart of it — the conscious, intentional silence.

When all three are true, that deliberate silence is the connivance.

Imagine a school security guard who notices that a group of students is sneaking alcohol into the school prom. He sees them clearly. He knows what's in their bags. But he has been slipped some money beforehand, so he simply turns his head and pretends he saw nothing.

The guard did not bring the alcohol. He did not drink it. But his deliberate silence made it all possible.

That is connivance.

The students smuggled the alcohol with the connivance of the security guard.

This is the most common way the word appears in real life. It always tells you two things at once:

  • Something wrong happened.
  • Someone who should have stopped it secretly allowed it instead.

More examples of the phrase in use:

  • "The prisoner escaped with the connivance of a corrupt warden." → The warden knew. The warden could have stopped it. The warden did nothing — maybe even quietly helped.
  • "The fraud went on for years with the connivance of senior management." → The bosses were aware of the fraud. They let it continue.
  • "The deal was struck with the connivance of the referee." → The referee quietly allowed a rule to be broken.
An Important Shade of Meaning: It Can Go Slightly Further

Connivance sits on a spectrum. At its lightest, it simply means turning a blind eye — pure silence. But it can stretch slightly further to include giving quiet, behind-the-scenes help that makes the wrongdoing easier, while still not being the one who does the wrong thing directly.

For example: A customs officer who does not just ignore smuggled goods but quietly signals to the smuggler which exit to use — that is still connivance, not a direct act of smuggling. The officer is still one step removed, operating in the shadows.

So connivance covers everything from passive silence to quiet, indirect assistance — as long as the person is not the main wrongdoer.
How It Feels — The Moral Weight

Connivance is considered morally serious because it makes you a partner in wrongdoing without getting your hands dirty directly. Society often judges silent bystanders with power harshly — because doing nothing, when you could act, is itself a choice.

The word carries a tone of betrayal of duty. A guard is supposed to guard. A manager is supposed to manage. A referee is supposed to enforce rules. When these people commit connivance, they have quietly abandoned their responsibility and handed it over to wrongdoing.
How Connivance Differs From Similar Words

These words are neighbours, but they are not the same:

Conspiracy — Here, people actively plan together to do something wrong. Everyone is in the room, talking, plotting. Connivance is quieter and more passive than this.

Complicity — Being complicit means you contributed to the wrongdoing in some way — you played a role, however small. Connivance can exist even if you contributed nothing at all — your silence alone is enough.

Collusion — Collusion means two or more parties secretly cooperate for a dishonest purpose, usually for mutual benefit. Connivance doesn't always require two parties working together — it can be one person alone, simply choosing not to act.

Negligence — Negligence means you failed to notice something you should have noticed, through carelessness. Connivance is different because the person did notice — they knew perfectly well. The failure was deliberate, not careless.
Connivance is the deliberate, knowing act of silently allowing something wrong to happen when you had both the awareness and the power to stop it.
If you ever forget the word, think of it this way: a conniver does not stab you — they simply hold the door open for the person who will, and then claim they saw nothing.
